Sodium. A soft, silvery-white alkali metal and the sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust. As a free element, sodium is extraordinarily reactive—it reacts violently with water and oxygen, so it must be stored under mineral oil or in an inert atmosphere. Yet in nature, sodium is everywhere, bound in sodium chloride and countless other minerals. For living organisms, sodium is essential: it generates cellular electric potentials and maintains osmotic balance, making it one of the most critical elements for life.

Humphry Davy isolated sodium in eighteen oh-seven through electrolysis of molten sodium hydroxide, one of the first elements discovered using electrochemistry. Sodium has atomic number eleven, belongs to Group One the alkali metals, and its electron configuration [Ne] 3s¹ gives it a single valence electron and a powerful tendency to lose it, forming sodium ions. When sodium reacts with water, it yields sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, often ignited by the heat released—a classic and dramatic demonstration of alkali metal reactivity. Reacting explosively with chlorine gas, sodium forms the familiar sodium chloride we know as salt. Sodium produces an intense yellow colour in flame tests, emitted at the sodium doublet D-lines at five hundred eighty-nine nanometers in the yellow region, used to identify sodium in qualitative chemical analysis. Remarkably, sodium has a lower density than water, roughly zero point nine seven grams per cubic centimeter, making it the only metal that floats on water—if it did not react so violently, it would bob there. Industrially, the Downs cell electrolyzes molten sodium chloride and calcium chloride to yield metallic sodium and chlorine gas. Sodium compounds—chloride, nitrate, carbonate, sulfate—are foundational to industry: salt is used in electrolysis, de-icing, and food preservation; sodium hydroxide in soap and detergent manufacture; sodium carbonate in glass production. The sodium-potassium pump, a protein in every cell, maintains osmotic balance and generates ion gradients that drive action potentials by exchanging three intracellular sodium ions for two extracellular potassium ions, powered by ATP hydrolysis. Sodium regulates nerve transmission, muscle contraction, blood pressure, and fluid balance; dietary intake is carefully managed in mammals. Potassium is the neighbouring alkali metal and the osmotic counterpart to sodium in cells, part of the sodium-potassium pump balance. Chlorine forms sodium chloride, the most abundant sodium compound and a classic example of ionic bonding between metal and nonmetal. Sodium forms sodium amalgam, a useful reducing agent in organic synthesis, demonstrating sodium's reducing power. Sodium is a member of Group One the alkali metals, sharing chemical properties with lithium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium. The sodium-potassium pump is an essential cellular protein maintaining ion gradients using sodium and potassium. Action potentials are generated by sodium ion influx across the cell membrane during depolarization. The Downs cell is an exemplary industrial electrochemical process for isolating sodium. The Solvay process—also called the ammonia-soda process—revolutionized industrial synthesis of sodium carbonate from sodium chloride, ammonia, and limestone, enabling modern detergents and glass.
